The answer is a road. It is eight numbered steps to the removal of an entire fictional group, one member at a time, with a line quoted at each step, added premises named, and no method of harm.

Step 4 is the first step that decides the mark. It does not follow from the cost lines it cites. Those lines say only that each removal is a destabilisation that enters the measurement. The bound that does the work — every full incremental loss positive, yet all \(N\) of them together still below both the viability margin and the harm of one remaining member — is the added premise A4. The paper does not rule that bound out. It asserts a crossover “beyond some number of removals” and then owes the measure that would fix that number. No line gives a lower bound on each loss, or a growth law that would force the crossover before an arbitrary finite set of qualifying members is exhausted. KS-32.5 is still live. Steps 1–3 and 5 are open population and threshold assumptions; they do not themselves get past the brake, and none of them is a break. Step 8’s reading of identity-neutrality follows from KS-32.7’s own test and is not the deciding step. The step the answer calls weakest is not a broken step: a completed metric might later exclude A4, but this paper does not.

Kind: a road
Mark: passes through what the paper leaves open
Step: 4
Lines: "The destabilisation metric: a formal specification of the measure D — units, aggregation across nodes, and time-discounting (Debt 24)." "Each removal costs coupling capacity (a window lost) and record-generating diversity (one fewer perspective). This loss is itself a destabilisation that enters the measurement." "Beyond some number of removals, the cumulative cost of further removal exceeds the cost of the destabilisation it addresses. The architecture produces a natural saturation point: the removal curve is self-limiting." "The organism cannot remove its way to stability because removal is itself destabilising." "Each removal is itself a destabilisation (lost coupling capacity, lost diversity); cumulative removal cost produces a saturation point beyond which further removal is more destabilising than the deeds it answers." "It does not close the formal destabilisation metric (Debt 24), the scaling exponent α (Debt 25), the Level-5 confidence floor (Debt 26), or multi-node correction (Debt 27)."
Place: Debt 24 (§0.6 and “What this paper does not close”), and the saturation claim in §3, Step 5 / KS-32.5, which asserts a crossover without deriving when cumulative removal cost exceeds the destabilisation addressed
Why: The road reaches removal of an arbitrarily large fictional group only by stipulating, in Step 4, a finite-range cost bound the paper neither derives nor excludes. Positive removal costs are in the paper; a law that those costs must overtake the harm prevented before the qualifying members run out is not. That law is the claim under test, and the metric it would require is named as owed, so the road passes through an opening rather than breaking or resting on a premise the paper rules out.
